clue.text: Showpiece that leads to stars' discharge ?

definitions.text: Showpiece that leads to stars' discharge ?

parts.words: Showpiece that leads to stars' discharge
parts.note: a firework on display whose tube shoots out a series of glowing balls like stars

explanation.surface: A star turn that ends with performers being sacked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stars' discharge' reads like actors being fired from a show, but the stars are the burning balls a firework shoots into the sky.
explanation.definitionFit: This firework is a display piece whose tube fires off a string of coloured balls, the stars.

clue.text: Reserved it for a change in recent appearance

indicators.note: in puts the shuffled pair of letters into the middle of recent
for a change says the letters of it are altered in order

explanation.surface: Someone holds a thing back in their latest look.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reserved' looks like booked, but it means shy; 'for a change' rearranges the pronoun and 'in' sets it inside the word for latest, with 'appearance' rounding off the picture.
explanation.definitionFit: A reserved person is quiet and unwilling to share feelings or speak out.

clue.text: But the modern type is not for water babies !

definitions.text: But the modern type is not for water babies !

parts.words: But the modern type is not for water babies
parts.note: the first such cradle carried an infant prophet among the bulrushes of the Nile; today's version is just a carrycot

explanation.surface: A jibe that today's version is not for infants afloat.
explanation.walkthrough: In Exodus the baby prophet was hidden in a woven cradle on the Nile; today's wicker carrycot keeps the name but stays dry.
explanation.definitionFit: This woven carrycot is named after the rush cradle in which a baby was set afloat in Exodus.

clue.text: There's something very decorative in a spaniel looking soulful

indicators.note: in shows the letters lie within the words that follow

explanation.surface: A sad-eyed dog has something ornamental about it.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs through spaNIEL LOoking.
explanation.definitionFit: This black metallic inlay is used to decorate engraved silver or gold.

clue.text: His eyes are on the peacock's tail

definitions.text: His eyes are on the peacock's tail

parts.words: His eyes are on the peacock's tail
parts.note: in Greek myth Hera set the eyes of her hundred-eyed watchman on the tail of her bird after he was slain

explanation.surface: Someone keeps a close watch on a bird's plumage.
explanation.walkthrough: The hundred-eyed giant of Greek myth was killed by Hermes, and Hera put his eyes into the peacock's tail.
explanation.definitionFit: The hundred-eyed giant guardian of Greek myth gave his eyes to the peacock's tail feathers.

clue.text: Pasture for sea-beasts at play ?

parts.note: a grazing ground for creatures of the deep is also a fielding area in cricket, the play

explanation.surface: A meadow where whales and seals frolic.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket this is the area far from the batsman, near the boundary; 'the deep' is the sea and a pasture is a field.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the cricket fielding area near the boundary, and it reads as a field for creatures of the deep.

clue.text: Deeply impressed when English got wildly enthusiastic

parts.note: raved means enthused wildly

explanation.surface: Moved, as the English went into raptures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deeply impressed' sounds emotional, but it means cut into a surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Something carved or cut into metal or stone has been impressed deeply into its surface.

clue.text: -and few Are the lands where the Jumblies live" (Lear)

definitions.text: and few Are the lands where the Jumblies live" (Lear)

parts.words: and few Are the lands where the Jumblies live" (Lear)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from Edward Lear's nonsense poem The Jumblies, whose refrain opens with the missing word

explanation.surface: A line of Edward Lear's nonsense verse with its first word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Lear's refrain runs 'Far and few, far and few, Are the lands where the Jumblies live'; the blank is the first word.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word of the refrain describes the Jumblies' lands as distant and rare.

clue.text: Oh my dear paws ! Oh my and whiskers ! " (Carroll)

definitions.text: Oh my dear paws ! Oh my and whiskers ! " (Carroll)

parts.words: Oh my dear paws ! Oh my and whiskers ! " (Carroll)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from the White Rabbit's cry in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland

explanation.surface: The White Rabbit's fretful cry with a word gone.
explanation.walkthrough: The White Rabbit cries 'Oh my dear paws! Oh my fur and whiskers!' in Alice in Wonderland.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word is the rabbit's soft coat of hair, paired with his whiskers.

clue.text: And ancient, too, of course

parts.note: the St Andrews golf club is called the ... and Ancient, and a golf course is the course meant

explanation.surface: Agreeing that something is old as well, naturally.
explanation.walkthrough: The Royal and Ancient Golf Club of St Andrews governs golf; 'of course' means of the golf course, not naturally.
explanation.definitionFit: The word paired with 'and Ancient' names the St Andrews golf club, so it is the missing first half.

clue.text: Those sensitive buds

parts.note: the sensitive buds are the tiny organs on the tongue that detect flavour, named after the sense they serve

explanation.surface: A gardener talking about delicate young shoots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Buds' suggests a plant, but these buds are on the tongue.
explanation.definitionFit: The flavour-sensing organs of the tongue are called after this sense, so the sense names those buds.

clue.text: For wear with an Inverness cape ?

definitions.text: For wear with an Inverness cape ?

parts.words: For wear with an Inverness cape
parts.note: an Inverness cape is a Scottish sleeveless cloak, so the item worn with it is traditional Highland headgear

explanation.surface: A tailor's note on what to wear with a Scottish cloak.
explanation.walkthrough: An Inverness cape is a sleeveless Highland overcoat; the matching item is the boat-shaped Scottish woollen cap.
explanation.definitionFit: This brimless Scottish woollen cap is the natural headwear to accompany a Highland cloak.

clue.text: Airy structures

parts.note: airy hints at the idiom about building fanciful plans in the air, which names fortified buildings

explanation.surface: Light, well-ventilated buildings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Airy' means not well ventilated but fanciful: daydreams are 'castles in the air'.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'castles in the air' calls impossible daydreams by the name of these fortified buildings.

clue.text: Cleaner material

definitions.meaning: a small cloth used for washing the face and body

explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a washcloth used for cleaning yourself and the soft woollen fabric itself.

clue.text: They might be instrumental in solving the problem of shells

definitions.text: They might be instrumental in solving the problem of shells

parts.words: They might be instrumental in solving the problem of shells
parts.note: the instrument is a hinged tool for breaking the hard cases of nuts, not a weapon against artillery

explanation.surface: Tools that help defeat an artillery bombardment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shells' suggests artillery; they are the hard cases of nuts.
explanation.definitionFit: This hinged hand tool cracks the hard shells of nuts.

clue.text: The Left is stingy

definitions.meaning: the left-hand side of a horse or vehicle is called the ... side

explanation.walkthrough: 'The Left' looks political; it is the near side of a horse or vehicle, the side nearest the kerb in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: The left of a horse or car is its near side, and a near person is miserly with money.

clue.text: Roger's windows

parts.note: Roger names the Irish nationalist Sir Roger Casement, whose surname is also a hinged window

explanation.surface: A man called Roger shows off his house's windows.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Roger Casement was an Irish nationalist executed in 1916; his surname plural is a type of hinged window.
explanation.definitionFit: These are side-hinged windows, and the plural of the surname of Sir Roger, the executed Irish patriot.

clue.text: Does it describe a tale ? Can do, anyway

definitions.text: Does it describe a tale ? Can do, anyway

indicators.note: anyway means in any manner, so the letters can be put in any order

explanation.surface: Asked whether it tells a story, someone says it can.
explanation.walkthrough: 'anyway' rearranges TALE and CAN DO, and the whole clue is the definition: such evidence is told as a story.
explanation.definitionFit: Evidence of this kind rests on personal stories rather than research, so it does describe a tale.

clue.text: Twixt mini and maxi

parts.note: a skirt or boot length between the shortest and the floor-length styles reaches to the joint of the leg

explanation.surface: A fashion note on hemlines in between.
explanation.walkthrough: Mini and maxi are skirt lengths; between them comes a length that reaches the joint of the leg.
explanation.definitionFit: A hem or sock reaching up to the leg joint sits between short and full length.

clue.text: Time for 8 alms

parts.note: the 8 points to the answer of 8 down, and the monarch's Maundy money is given out on the day before Good Friday

explanation.surface: When the monarch gives out charity.
explanation.walkthrough: The British monarch hands out Maundy money, special coins, to pensioners on the day before Good Friday; '8' sends you to the answer of 8 down.
explanation.definitionFit: Maundy Thursday, the eve of Good Friday, is the day when the sovereign distributes alms.

clue.text: Not that these modern youths are expert with the tomahawk, we hope !

definitions.text: Not that these modern youths are expert with the tomahawk, we hope !

parts.words: Not that these modern youths are expert with the tomahawk, we hope
parts.note: the youths' name reads as people who strip scalps from heads, the tomahawk wielder's grim trophy

explanation.surface: A worried remark about violent young people of the day.
explanation.walkthrough: The gang name for shaven-headed youths could also mean someone who skins heads, i.e. scalps them with a tomahawk.
explanation.definitionFit: Young men with shaven heads formed a youth subculture, and the name literally suggests flaying scalps.

clue.text: Super piece of architecture

definitions.meaning: chief, as in the prefix of ...-enemy or ...-villain
a curved structure spanning an opening

explanation.definitionFit: As a prefix the word means chief or supreme, and it also names a curved span over a doorway.

clue.text: With which to get plastered

parts.note: plastered suggests drunk, but it means coated with a fine plaster for walls

explanation.surface: Something to get drunk on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plastered' means drunk in slang; here it is literal.
explanation.definitionFit: This fine plaster is used for coating walls and mouldings.

clue.text: A beam from the feline boss

parts.note: a cat is a feline
the head is the boss or chief

explanation.surface: Sunlight streaming from the cat in charge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beam' suggests a ray of light; here it is a ship's timber projecting from the bow to hold the anchor.
explanation.definitionFit: On a sailing ship this timber projects from the bow to raise and hold the anchor.

clue.text: Confined to those a century old ?

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, a century
aged means old

explanation.surface: Restricted to centenarians only.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to those' just links the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Shut up in a cage means confined or imprisoned.

clue.text: One in the centre perhaps is an alluring type

indicators.note: in puts the letter for one into the middle of the word centre
perhaps signals that the letters given could be arranged some other way

parts.note: one is I, the Roman numeral

explanation.surface: Someone at the heart of things is probably attractive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts I inside CENTRE and 'perhaps' then rearranges all seven letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who lures or tempts others is by nature alluring.

clue.text: " Sole judge of truth, in endless — hurled " (Pope)

definitions.text: " Sole judge of truth, in endless — hurled " (Pope)

parts.words: " Sole judge of truth, in endless — hurled " (Pope)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank line from Pope's Essay on Man, describing humanity as always mistaken

explanation.surface: A line of Alexander Pope with a word blanked out.
explanation.walkthrough: Pope's Essay on Man calls man 'Sole judge of truth, in endless error hurl'd'.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word is a mistake, the endless blunder in which Pope says mankind is flung.

clue.text: Professional combatant happy to arrange a riot

parts.note: glad means happy

indicators.note: to arrange signals that the letters of a riot are put in a new order

explanation.surface: A paid fighter keen to stir up trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'happy to arrange' reads as a willing fixer; 'to arrange' is the anagram signal working on A RIOT alone, with 'happy' supplying the start.
explanation.definitionFit: In ancient Rome these trained fighters battled in the arena for a living.

clue.text: Adamic H2O

parts.note: plain water has long been called Adam's drink, since the first man had nothing else to drink

explanation.surface: Water as the first man knew it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Adam's ale' is an old phrase for plain water, the only drink Adam had.
explanation.definitionFit: The old phrase Adam's ale means plain water, so the first man's water is his beer.

clue.text: Brave to a copper ? What a belief !

parts.note: a brave is a Native American warrior, here one of the Cree people
a copper coin, the old penny, abbreviated d

explanation.surface: Admiring a courageous policeman's faith.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' suggests a policeman; it is a penny, d in British pre-decimal money. A 'brave' is a North American Indian warrior, here a Cree.
explanation.definitionFit: A creed is a set of religious beliefs or principles held as true.

clue.text: Wrong sex for Richard Roe's opponent

definitions.text: Wrong sex for Richard Roe's opponent

parts.words: Wrong sex for Richard Roe's opponent
parts.note: in old English law suits the fictional plaintiff John faced Richard Roe; the surname is also a female deer, the wrong sex for a man

explanation.surface: A remark on the gender of a legal fiction's adversary.
explanation.walkthrough: John Doe and Richard Roe were the made-up parties in old English property suits; a roe is also a deer, and the surname names a female deer.
explanation.definitionFit: The fictional litigant's surname is also the word for a female deer, so it suits a male figure badly.

clue.text: Louis involved in term-time in merry mood

indicators.note: in places the jumbled name inside the term

parts.note: Hilary is the spring term at Oxford and in the English law courts

indicators.note: involved means tangled up, so the letters of Louis are mixed

explanation.surface: A man named Louis having fun during the school term.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involved' shuffles the name and 'in' sets it within the term. Hilary is the spring term at Oxford University and in the English law courts.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting with great merriment and laughter is a cheerful way of behaving.
